INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are a group of social scientists specializing
in epidemiology, survey research, data science,
economics, and criminology.  Collectively, the amici
have more than a century of experience conducting
empirical research on firearm ownership and use and
have published more than 300 peer-reviewed journal
articles related to these issues.  They file this brief on
behalf of themselves as individuals, not as
representatives of any institution.
Deborah Azrael is the Director of Research of the
Harvard Injury Control Research Center, with over
25 years of grant-funded leadership in firearm
violence and injury surveillance.  Named by The Trace
as one of the ten Americans who shaped the gun
debate and recipient of the American Public Health
Association’s Excellence in Science Award, she codirected the pilot for what became the National
Violent Death Reporting System—a comprehensive
50-state surveillance system tracking all homicides,
suicides, and unintentional firearm deaths—and has
authored over 150 peer-reviewed articles on firearm
ownership, storage practices, and suicide prevention.
Professor Philip Cook is Professor Emeritus of
Public Policy and Economics at Duke University, a
member of the National Academy of Medicine, and
the recipient of the Stockholm Prize in Criminology—

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, amici state that no
counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in part and
no entity or person, aside from amici or their counsel, made any
monetary contribution intended to fund its preparation or

2

internationally recognized as the highest honor in the
field—for decades of pioneering research on gun
violence and its societal effects.  Among the first
scholars to systematically study gun violence
prevention, he has authored landmark books and
numerous peer-reviewed articles on the costs,
consequences, and regulation of firearm availability.
Professor David Hemenway is Professor of Health
Policy at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public
Health and Director of the Harvard Injury Control
Research Center.  Recognized by the Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention with its 20 for 20
Leadership Award as one of the twenty most
influential injury and violence professionals over a
two-decade span, he has authored over 200 peerreviewed articles on injury and firearm violence,
alongside seminal books such as Private Guns, Public
Health.
Professor Matthew Miller is University
Distinguished Professor of Health Sciences and
Epidemiology at Northeastern University, Adjunct
Professor of Epidemiology at the Harvard T.H. Chan
School of Public Health, and Co-Director of the
Harvard Injury Control Research Center.  Elected to
the National Academy of Medicine for foundational
epidemiological research establishing the causal link
between firearm access and heightened suicide risk,
Dr. Miller has authored more than 200 peer-reviewed
papers related to firearm ownership, use, and the
medical, social, and public-health-related risks and
benefits of firearm ownership.
Oren Tirschwell is a Data Scientist at the

3

University of Chicago Crime Lab.  He applies data
science and machine learning techniques to better
understand complex social science and public policy
questions.  His research co vers survey analysis on
various firearm-related instruments (blending
inferential and predictive techniques), U.S. crime
data analyses, and analysis of federal violenceprevention funding in major cities.
Amici’s shared interest in these cases is in the
integrity of the empirical record on which courts rely.
Amici have devoted their careers to conducting
empirical research on firearm ownership and use,
including published, peer-reviewed work assessing
the survey evidence Petitioners press here.  Amici
therefore do not come to th ese questions for the first
time in this litigation, and they submit this brief to
assist the Court in distinguishing evidence that can
bear constitutional weight from evidence that cannot.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Petitioners and aligned amici ask this Court to
resolve a constitutional question of national
importance by relying heavily on a small set of
contested empirical claims about ownership and use
of AR-15 platform and simila r semiautomatic rifles.
See, e.g. , Viramontes Pet. Merits Br. 11–12, 34–35;
Grant, Pet. for Cert. 9–10; Br. of Amicus Curiae Nat’l
Shooting Sports Found. 6; Br. of Amicus Curiae
United States 21.  Chief among their sources are two
non-peer-reviewed papers th at report the results of
surveys conducted by Professor William English: the
first from 2021, and the second from 2026.

4

At the threshold, the English Surveys fail to
establish that AR-15-style rifles are “commonly used”
in the sense contemplated by the Second Amendment.
“Common use” is not judged merely by a present-day
snapshot; the question is whether an arm has proven
itself, across time, to be the sort of weapon ordinary
citizens actually rely upon for lawful purposes, such
as self-defense.  See Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438,
450 (4th Cir. 2024) (Wilkinson, J.) (en banc), cert.
denied sub nom. Snope v. Brown , 145 S. Ct. 1534
(2025).  Yet neither English Survey speaks to that
question.  And as explained below, the surveys do not
even succeed at providing a current-day snapshot of
gun ownership.
Professor English is not a disinterested source
whose work Petitioners happened to find.  He is a
participant in this litigation, having filed an amicus
brief in these consolidated  cases urging the result
Petitioners seek, just as he did in New York State Rifle
& Pistol Assn., Inc. v. Bruen.  See Nos. 25-238, 25-566,
Br. of Amici Curiae Prof. William English & Center
for Human Liberty Supporting Petitioners; No. 20-
843, Br. of Amici Curiae William English, Ph.D., and
the Center for Human Liberty in Support of
Petitioners.  In fact, the 2026 Survey was still in the
field only weeks before Peti tioners’ merits brief was
filed, and English did not issue his report until four
days before that filing.  Likewise, the 2021 Survey
was fielded in the weeks before this Court granted
certiorari in Bruen.
Nor is Professor English an expert in firearm
ownership and use patterns or in survey research.
Indeed, English has never pu blished anything in the

5

peer-reviewed literature related to firearms, and his
sole prior published research using survey data he
collected is limited to a single small, non-probability
sample on a topic that has nothing to do with firearm
ownership or use.  See William English, Demystifying
trust: Experimental evidence from Cambodia and
Thailand, 24 J. of Theoretical Politics 172 (2012)
(considering a two-page questionnaire administered
to 97 high school students in Thailand and Cambodia,
entirely unrelated to firearms).  His research on
firearms appears to have begun only in 2021 in
connection with an NRA-backed lawsuit.   See Mike
McIntire & Jodi Kantor, The Gun Lobby’s Hidden
Hand in the 2nd Amendment Battle, N.Y. Times (June
18, 2024).2
The 2021 Survey—which purported to provide
estimates of AR-15 and similar rifle ownership and
use—was marred by defects, as recognized by judges
and scholars, including amici, which render its
findings unreliable.  See Ass’n of N.J. Rifle & Pistol
Clubs, Inc. v. Att’y Gen. , 183 F.4th 211, 303 n.10 (3d
Cir. 2026) (Krause, J., dissenting); Barnett v. Raoul ,
2024 WL 4719468, at *7 (S.D . Ill. Nov. 8, 2024);
Deborah Azrael, Joseph Blocher, Philip J. Cook,
David Hemenway & Matthew Miller, A Critique of
Findings on Gun Ownership, Use, and Imagined Use
From the 2021 National Firearms Survey: Response to
William English, 78 SMU L. Rev. 239 (2025).
The 2026 Survey is expressly framed as a response
to critics of the 2021 Survey.  But the new Survey
repeats many of the design choices that made its

2 https://perma.cc/SR5P-NERX.

6

predecessor unreliable.  It again primes respondents
towards affirmative answers and relies on an opt-in
survey methodology, rendering it non-representative
of gun owners nationwide.  Further, English’s results
cannot be reconciled with his previous results,
independent surveys, firearm production data, the
effects of long-standing stat e bans, or public records
of concealed-carry permits.  Finally, the 2026 Survey
provides this Court with no evidence of the frequency
with which AR-15 and similarly styled rifles are used
for lawful self-defense.
In sum, neither the 2026 Survey nor its
predecessor can support Pe titioners’ efforts to
invalidate the laws at issue.  The methodological
defects of the 2026 Survey render it unreliable, and it
cannot show that AR-15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles are in common use.
ARGUMENT
I. The English Surveys Cannot Be Used To
Establish “Common Use,” As They
Provide No More Than A Deeply Flawed
Present-Day Snapshot Of Firearm
Markets
The Second Amendment “does not protect those
weapons not typically possessed by law-abiding
citizens for lawful purposes.”  District of Columbia v.
Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 625 (2008)  (emphasis added).
“Drawing from ... historical tradition,” it “protects
only the carrying of weapons that are those ‘in
common use at the time.’”  New York State Rifle &
Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1, 47 (2022)
(citation omitted).  Those are empirical questions:

7

how many law-abiding citizens keep a given arm, and
for what purposes they use it.  Answering them
requires reliable evidence.
The “common use” inquiry is not satisfied by a
present-day snapshot of ownership or use.  In
Bianchi, for example, Judge Wilkinson explained that
“[a]rms typically used by average citizens for selfdefense are generally within the ambit of the Second
Amendment, presumably because these arms had
proven over time to effectively amplify an individual’s
power to protect himself without empowering him to
single-handedly reign terror upon a community.”  111
F.4th at 450 (emphasis added).  Assessing use “over
time” helps ensure that “arms manufacturers” cannot
“secure constitutional immunity for their products so
long as they distribute a sufficient quantity before
legislatures can react.”  Id. at 450, 461.
A rule under which a weapon acquires
constitutional protection by proliferating before a
legislature responds would improperly transform
legislative inaction or de lay into a forfeiture of
legislative authority, tying the hands of present and
future legislators.  Justice Barrett warned against
considering legislative inaction in the historicaltradition inquiry, as demanding “overly specific”
historical analogues to challenged laws “assumes that
founding-era legislatures maximally exercised their
power to regulate, thereby adopting a ‘use it or lose it’
view of legislative authority.”  United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 739–40 (2024) (Barrett, J.,
concurring).  Her observation addresses a different
aspect of the Second Amendment analysis, but the
assumption she rejects is the same one: that a

8

legislature that has not yet acted somehow, at some
ill-defined point, thereby loses the power to act.  Such
“assumptions are flawed, and originalism does not
require them.”  Id. at 740.
Whatever evidence might satisfy the common-use
inquiry, it is manifest that neither English Survey
supplies it.  Neither asks when respondents acquired
AR-15 or similarly styled rifles nor how long they
have owned them.  See William English, 2021
National Firearms Survey: Updated Analysis
Including Types of Firearms Owned 33 (Georgetown
McDonough Sch. of Bus. Rsch. Paper No. 4109494,
May 13, 2022), https://pe rma.cc/E8H9-N6RZ (“2021
Survey”); William English, 2026 National Firearms
Survey: Results from the Second Wave, Including
Current Ownership of AR-15 Style Rifles, Other
“Assault Weapons,” and Magazines that Hold More
than 10 Rounds 57 (Georgetown Univ. Working
Paper, Aug. 2026), https://perma.cc/L535-DTQF
(“2026 Survey”).  And as the balance of this brief
explains, the surveys do not reliably establish even
the present-day ownership they purport to measure.
In short, even setting aside the critical
methodological defects in the English Surveys, they
fail to provide the necessary evidence of “common use”
that this Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence
requires.  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 47.
II. Reliance On The English Studies Is
Misplaced
The linchpin of Petitioners’ case is that AR-15-
style rifles are “in common use and therefore
protected by the Second Am endment.”  Pet. Br. 34.

9

They rely heavily on Professor William English’s
Surveys of gun owners to establish how many
Americans own these rifles, why they own them, and
how often rifles are used for defense.  Id. at 11–12,
34–35.
The English Surveys do not reliably or accurately
support Petitioners’ claims about firearm ownership
and use, failing in both methodology and analysis.
The surveys were tailored for litigation and have
never been peer reviewed.  English drew his
respondents from opt-in online panels, which cannot
be assumed  to represent the U.S. population overall,
or the population of gun owners.  His key ownership
question primes respondents to provide preferred
answers, and English’s results conflict with one
another, as well as with independent data.  Any
empirical evidence this Court considers must reliably
and accurately measure firearm ownership and use.
The English surveys fall far short.
A. The Surveys Have Never Been
Tested By Peer Review
Neither English Survey has been peer reviewed—
both were circulated as working papers.  2026 Survey
1; see id.  at 49 (listing the 2021 report as a
Georgetown McDonough School of Business research
paper).  Nor did the Surveys arise from a neutral
inquiry.  English’s survey work began as research for
an NRA-backed lawsuit. 3  Only the 2026 Survey
names a funder—the Wealth of Nations Institute. 4

3 See McIntire & Kantor, supra n. 2.
4 According to the organization, it “conducts and promotes
scholarly research and education on the importance of markets,

10

2026 Survey 5.
Parties cannot put forward unpublished, nonpeer-reviewed studies they find most beneficial and
demand the Court ignore the studies’ defects.  Nonadjudicative facts—including empirical evidence on
the ownership and use of firearms—are a legitimate
and often necessary part of appellate decisionmaking.  As Judge Dyk of  the Federal Circuit has
explained, appellate courts, “including the Supreme
Court,” regularly consider such facts in formulating
legal rules, and their use is “legitimate and common.”5
But reliability and accuracy are paramount.  Courts
“should consider whether a study was peer reviewed
or whether it has been accepted and cited approvingly
by experts in the field,” and “should be wary of
untested empirical statements and predictions
provided by interested parties.”6  Courts “should treat
the results of surveys with particular caution” and
“carefully assess the methodology and
representativeness of surveys.”  Jack Daniel’s Props.,
Inc. v. VIP Prods. LLC , 599 U.S. 140, 163 (2023)
(Sotomayor, J., concurring).  This Court should not
risk “accept[ing] the studie s’ findings on faith,
without examining their methodology at all.”  Sykes
v. United States , 564 U.S. 1, 31 (2011) (Scalia, J.,

individual rights, and peace.”  Wealth of Nations Institute,
https://perma.cc/MB3C-FQMP.  It  was formed in 2024, and its
website identifies no officers, donors, or other projects.  See id.
5 Timothy B. Dyk, The Role of Non-Adjudicative Facts in
Judicial Decisionmaking, 76 Stan. L. Rev. Online 10, 11, 22–23
(2023), https://perma.cc/D9UA-SRQB.
6 Id.

11

dissenting), overruled on other grounds by Johnson v.
United States, 576 U.S. 591 (2015).
The English Surveys raise each of these red flags.
Absent peer review, the Court cannot be confident
that English’s findings reflect sound methodology.
And the origins of Englis h’s survey work demand
scrutiny, as it “originated as research for a National
Rifle Association-backed lawsuit,” rather than an
examination of current trends, while English
reportedly “has received tens of thousands of dollars
as a paid expert for gun rights advocates.”7
At the certiorari stage, Petitioners relied on the
2021 Survey.  Pet. for Cert. 8.  Notably, only after this
Court granted certiorari did English produce the 2026
Survey.  See 2026 Survey 1.  Petitioners cite a version
dated August 24, four days before they filed their
merits brief.  Pet. Br. 11.  The study thus has not been
subjected to meaningful examination.  Yet Petitioners
ask the Court to accept it s findings as reliable
empirical evidence.  “Supreme Court briefs are an
inappropriate place to develop the key facts in a case.”
Sykes, 564 U.S. at 31 (Scalia, J., dissenting).  But that
is precisely what Petitioners attempt to do by
invoking English’s survey.
Courts are already aware of the issues posed by
English’s original survey.  Addressing the 2021
Survey in a challenge to I llinois’s restrictions on AR-
15s and other semiautomatic firearms, the district
court found that “the methodological errors and
inherent biases raise concerns about the reliability of

7 See McIntire & Kantor, supra n.2.

12

Professor English’s survey relating to his
determination that various challenged semiautomatic
firearms and large-capacity magazines are in
common use.”  Barnett, 2024 WL 4719468, at *7.  It
“elect[ed] not to rely on the English Survey in
resolving any questions of fact.”  Id . (emphasis
omitted).
A court reviewing the Connecticut law challenged
here emphasized that the 2021 survey asked whether
respondents had “ever owned” a large-capacity
magazine, not whether they currently did, and that
respondents’ stated reasons for owning assault
weapons did “not demonstrate that assault weapons
and LCMs possess characteristics that make them
well-suited for self-defense.”  Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts.
v. Lamont, 685 F. Supp. 3d 63, 95 n.22, 97 (D. Conn.
2023) (emphasis omitted), aff’d, 153 F.4th 213 (2d Cir.
2025).  More fundamentally, the survey is “an
unpublished, non-peer-reviewed summary of an
online survey” with “hidden sponsorship funding” and
a failure to “fully and openly disclose the
measurement tools.”  Ass’n of N.J. Rifle & Pistol
Clubs, Inc., 183 F.4th at 303 n.10 (Krause, J.,
dissenting).
The 2026 Survey remains an unpublished, nonpeer-reviewed report that is untested legally or
scientifically.  These defect s make scrutiny essential
before its results are employed to inform the scope of
a constitutional right.  As explained below, the
questions, the sampling, an d the results each give

13

concrete reasons to doubt its reliability.8
B. English Primes Respondents
Toward Affirmative Answers
Statements placed immediately before a survey
question can influence the answers. 9  English
acknowledges this risk, purporting to design
screening questions to avoid “priming respondents
with the sensitive topic of the survey.”  2026 Survey
6.  But he courted that very risk in the questions that
matter most.
Leading questions and explanatory preambles can
create “demand characteristics”—cues that reveal
what a study seeks to establish and may cause
respondents to “echo that information back” in their
answers.10  The Federal Judicial Center’s surveyresearch guide warns that respondents who know a
survey’s purpose or sponsor “may adjust their

8 English’s dataset (which includes the ordering and text of
questions) is available through download at: English, William,

https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/QNSWP1, Harvard Dataverse, V1,

To summarize: When Americans defend
themselves with a firearm, they do so overwhelmingly
with a handgun, and rarely with an AR-15 platform
or similar rifle.  Nearly everyone who owns one of
these rifles already owns a handgun; not having an
AR-15 would do little to affect their ability to defend
themselves with a gun.  These rifles are used in about
1% of justifiable homicides,  but in about 25% of the
public mass shootings that terrorize American
communities.

For the foregoing reasons, the Court should affirm
